pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; Rain & Puddles (CONCEPTUAL, 0.08): rain falls from clouds; puddles disappear because the water goes back into the air; water moves around — up into the sky and back down again (a first, intuitive water cycle).
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 weather observation (Y1 'Seasonal changes' — rain as weather); the evaporation/water-cycle mechanism is formally KS2 Year 4 'States of matter' (evaporation & condensation in the water cycle). At 5-7 this is a pre-cursor intuition, not the formal cycle. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS2-1 weather observation (VERIFIED verbatim); the water-cycle mechanism proper is grade-2/5 (2-ESS2-3 water is solid/liquid; 5 water cycle). Keep it observational-plus-one-idea (the puddle's water went UP), not a full cycle.
• Operational details — The powerful, age-appropriate insight is CONSERVATION: the puddle's water did not simply 'vanish' or only 'soak into the ground' — it went up into the air (as invisible vapour) and can come back down as rain. Make the disappearing puddle the hook. Keep 'evaporation/condensation' as everyday language ('the sun dries it up, the water goes into the air') — the formal words arrive with The Water Cycle (7-9) which this feeds. Prerequisite: Types of Weather (rain). Evidence: rain falls from clouds; puddles disappear because water goes into the air; water goes up and comes back down repeatedly.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/observational): the child states that rain comes from clouds and explains a drying puddle as the water going UP into the air (not just vanishing or only soaking away), grasping the basic up-and-down movement — described concretely, without the formal evaporation/condensation vocabulary.
bestPractices: Hook on the everyday mystery 'where does the puddle GO?' and land the conservation idea — the water went up into the air, it didn't cease to exist — which is the key intellectual move at this age.
Use real, observable evidence: mark a puddle's edge in the morning and check it shrinking by afternoon; put water in a saucer in the sun; breathe on a cold window — first-hand before any diagram.
Keep vocabulary everyday ('the sun warms the water and it goes into the air as tiny bits you can't see') and reserve 'evaporation/condensation/precipitation' for the 7-9 Water Cycle this leads into.
Make the invisibility explicit and non-magical: the water becomes vapour we can't see — counter 'it just disappeared' with 'it's still there, just spread out in the air'.
Close the loop simply: water that went up can come back down as rain, so it goes round — a gentle first cycle, not a labelled diagram.
Connect to children's experience (wet washing drying, wet hair, steam from a bath) so the idea generalises beyond puddles.
keyRepresentations: A time-lapse puddle shrinking under the sun, with a marked starting edge — the observable-conservation hook.
Tiny 'invisible' water dots rising from the puddle to a cloud, then falling back as rain — a simple up-and-down loop.
Cloud→rain→puddle→(up again) as a small circular arrow diagram, kept wordless/iconic.
Everyday analogues: drying washing, a steamy mirror, a saucer of water left in the sun.
commonMisconceptions: 'The puddle just disappeared / dried up into nothing.' — The water still exists; it moved into the air as invisible vapour (conservation).
'The water only soaked into the ground.' — Some may, but a puddle on tarmac also shrinks because water goes UP into the air; both can happen.
'Clouds are made of smoke/cotton wool.' — Clouds are tiny water droplets; at this age keep it to 'clouds are made of water' without over-detailing.
'Rain comes from the sky' with no link to clouds — make the cloud→rain connection explicit.
'The sun boils the puddle away' — evaporation happens at ordinary warmth, not boiling; avoid implying it must be hot enough to boil.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach the intuitive precursor to the water cycle: rain falls from clouds, and a drying puddle's water goes UP into the air (as invisible vapour we can't see), not out of existence. The core intellectual move is conservation — the water moved, it didn't vanish or only soak away — and that water can come back down as rain, a first up-and-down loop. Keep vocabulary everyday ('the sun warms the water and it goes into the air'); reserve 'evaporation/condensation/precipitation' for the later Water Cycle topic this feeds. Ground everything in first-hand, observable evidence before any diagram.

activities.title: The vanishing puddle: where did the water go?
feedback: If the child says 'it disappeared / dried up into nothing', respond: 'It's still there — just spread out in the air as tiny bits too small to see. Water in the air can come back down as rain somewhere — watch it happen in our pretend scene.'

If the child says 'it all soaked into the ground', acknowledge some water can soak in, then point out a puddle on hard ground (tarmac or a saucer) still shrinks because water also goes UP into the air.
When the child says the water went up into the air and came back down as rain, affirm: 'Yes — the water was never lost, it went up and came back down again.'
activities.rationale: A change-over-time process is made concrete when the learner sees the water relocate rather than being told it vanished, which targets the conservation misconception directly. Marking a real puddle's edge gives observable evidence of shrinking. The rising dots and the refill are a simplified pretend model of the up-and-down loop: real water vapour is invisible, spreads out, forms clouds higher up, and falls as rain in many places. An optional interactive scene (draggable sun or time control, a receding marked edge, rising water dots to a cloud, tap-to-rain refill, and a 'where did the water go?' reveal) can make the mechanism felt by letting the child drive it; this is one way to present it, not a required medium.
sourceClaims: Common young-learner water misconceptions: a drying puddle 'disappears into nothing' or only 'soaks into the ground', and that evaporation requires boiling; teaching should foreground conservation (water moves into the air as invisible vapour).
learnerActions: Watch (or drive) a fresh puddle after rain: mark where the puddle's edge starts, then let the sun warm it over time and watch the puddle shrink back from the marked line until it's gone.

In a pretend or animated scene, watch dots that stand for tiny bits of water rise from the puddle into the air. Explain that in real life we cannot see these bits, and that they spread out and only form clouds much higher up where the air is cold, not as a cloud right above the puddle.
Answer the prompt 'Where did the water go?' out loud before any explanation is given.

In the pretend scene, make it rain from the cloud and watch water come back down to refill the puddle. Explain that in real life rain falls in lots of places, so the same water does not land back in the same puddle.
Say in the child's own words where the water went and whether it was lost.
activities.intendedInsight: The puddle's water did not disappear or cease to exist — it went up into the air (as invisible vapour) and can come back down again as rain. Water moves up and down; it is conserved.

activities.title: First-hand drying investigation (saucer in the sun)
feedback: If the child predicted the water would be 'gone', point to the droplets on the film: 'The water was caught, not destroyed — here it is again.'
Draw out the pre-observation reason as the key tell: what the child predicted and why matters more than the final answer.
Reinforce: the water spread out into the air; the clear lid let us trap it and see it return as drops.
activities.rationale: Direct observation with a captured-vapour outcome confronts the 'gone forever' idea with physical evidence. The pre-observation reasoning surfaces the child's actual model. Using real materials first supports building intuition before any diagram. Observe the saucer and the droplets on the film — never look toward the sun.
sourceClaims: Common young-learner water misconceptions: a drying puddle 'disappears into nothing' or only 'soaks into the ground', and that evaporation requires boiling; teaching should foreground conservation (water moves into the air as invisible vapour).
learnerActions: Put the same shallow amount of water in two saucers, cover one with cling film and leave the other uncovered, and leave both in a warm or sunny spot.
Before observing, predict what will happen to the water and say WHY (many predict it will simply dry up and be gone) — state the reason out loud.
Return later to look at the underside of the film and describe the droplets that have collected there.

Discuss: the water in the open saucer went down or disappeared, but under the film it stayed in and droplets formed on the film. Where did those droplets come from, and where did the open saucer's water go?
activities.intendedInsight: Water that leaves the saucer isn't destroyed — it rises as invisible vapour and can be caught again as droplets on a cover, showing it still exists.

activities.title: Invisible water you can show
feedback: If the child rejects the air explanation because the vapour can't be seen, use the fogged mirror / cold glass to show the unseen water reappearing as droplets.
Affirm everyday links: 'Your wet hair dries the same way — the water goes into the air.'
activities.rationale: Addressing the 'if it were in the air we'd see it' misconception needs a demonstration that makes invisible water reappear on a cold surface. Connecting to familiar drying experiences helps the idea generalise beyond puddles.
sourceClaims: Common young-learner water misconceptions: a drying puddle 'disappears into nothing' or only 'soaks into the ground', and that evaporation requires boiling; teaching should foreground conservation (water moves into the air as invisible vapour).
learnerActions: Breathe on a cold window or mirror and watch it fog, then describe where the mist came from.
Connect to everyday experiences: wet washing drying, wet hair drying, and the misty 'steam' over a hot bath (tiny drops of water we can see, made when invisible water in the air cools).
Explain why we usually can't see the water that goes into the air, even though it is still there.
activities.intendedInsight: Water can be in the air as invisible vapour; we can make it visible again on a cold surface, which makes 'unseen water' believable and non-magical.

activities.title: Puddle detective: explain it yourself
feedback: Says the water went up into the air as invisible vapour, still exists, and can fall again as rain — describing the up-and-down loop, and predicts droplets under a covering lid: full understanding; affirm and extend.
Says the water went into the air but treats it as a one-way disappearance: prompt 'Could that same water come back down? How?' to build the return leg.
Says the water is gone/dried up into nothing, or only that it sank away: return to the vanishing-puddle observation and the captured-droplets demo.
Note: a child articulating the explanation shows reasoning, but saying it unprompted here does not by itself prove the hands-on observation was done — pair with the first-hand activities.
activities.rationale: Asking the child to explain elicits their own reasoning and reveals which specific model they hold. It pairs well with the first-hand observations rather than replacing them; a short tap-to-reveal recap loop (cloud→rain→puddle→up again, with a 'where does the puddle go?' flap) can consolidate afterward.
learnerActions: Respond to a curious prompt — 'There was a puddle here this morning, and nobody tipped it out or mopped it up. Where did it go, and is it gone forever?'
Give a full explanation in the child's own words.

Answer probe questions: 'If the water went into the air, why can't we see it?', 'Could that same water come back down to the ground? How?', 'What if we covered the puddle with a clear lid — where would the water go then?'
activities.intendedInsight: The child can articulate the conservation idea and the up-and-back-down loop unprompted, distinguishing 'moved into the air' from 'gone'.

constraints: Keep this observational-plus-one-idea: rain comes from clouds, and the puddle's water went UP. Do not present a full labelled evaporation–condensation–precipitation cycle at this age.
Use everyday language only; reserve 'evaporation', 'condensation', 'precipitation' for the later (7-9) Water Cycle topic this feeds into.

Prerequisite: Types of Weather (rain). This feeds the formal water cycle, which is UK DfE KS2 Year 4 'States of matter'; in US NGSS related ideas appear in grades 2 and 5, with the water cycle formally at middle school — not expected formally at 5-7.
Avoid implying evaporation needs boiling: water goes into the air at ordinary warmth, not only when hot enough to boil.
Keep clouds simple: 'clouds are made of water (tiny droplets)'; avoid 'smoke/cotton wool' descriptions without over-detailing.

A 1–2 item multiple-choice check with a clear 'goes into the air' option can check the key idea after an activity, but recognition alone does not build the conservation intuition or elicit the child's own explanation; word options so 'it disappeared' is not reinforced.
A tap-to-reveal lift-flap loop communicates the idea but presents a pre-set answer rather than letting the child drive and observe the change; use it as a recap, not the primary build.
For any sun-and-puddle observation, look at the puddle, its marked edge, or droplets on a lid/cold surface — never ask a child to look at or toward the sun.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row (DfE KS2 placement and the Ohio State misconceptions reference, both from prior-session memory, not re-fetched). Treat curriculum placement and misconception specifics as unconfirmed this session.

The legacy entry asserted a static image 'can only assert' conservation while an interactive 'achieves' it, and that dialogue 'under-delivers'/the phenomenon is 'best SHOWN'; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to describe affordances rather than medium superiority.

The assess field's correctAnswer uses 'evaporated' and formal vocabulary; at learner level this is kept as everyday language ('goes into the air'), with formal vocabulary deferred per the pedagogy notes — a minor tension between the assess wording and the age-appropriate vocabulary constraint, not an error to carry into child-facing text.

assess.poeTask: Put a shallow puddle of water in a saucer, cover it with cling film, and leave it in a sunny spot. Ask children to predict what will happen to the water and WHY — many predict it will simply dry up and be gone. Observing droplets collecting on the underside of the film confronts the 'gone forever' idea: the water is caught, not destroyed. The pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If the water went into the air, why can't we see it?
Could that same water ever come back down to the ground? How?
What if we covered the puddle with a clear lid — where would the water go then?
assess.correctAnswer: The water went up into the air as invisible water vapour — it evaporated. It isn't gone or destroyed, it's just spread out in the air where we can't see it. Later that same water can form clouds and fall back down as rain.

errorPatterns.pattern: Evaporation as disappearance — 'it dried up and is just gone'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish conservation: the water changed into invisible vapour and is still there; capture it under a lid to show it comes back as droplets.
errorPatterns.distractor: The water dried up and disappeared — it's gone now.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the water no longer exists / vanished into nothing

errorPatterns.pattern: Only soaks into the ground — denies the air route
errorPatterns.nextMove: Acknowledge some soaks in, but show a puddle on solid ground (or a saucer) still vanishes — that water went up into the air.
errorPatterns.distractor: It all soaked down into the ground, none went into the air.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says all the water sank into the ground and none went into the air

errorPatterns.pattern: Water in the air must be visible — 'if it were in the air we'd see it'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce invisible water vapour with the fogged-mirror / cold-glass demo so unseen water becomes believable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the air explanation because the vapour can't be seen

responseLevels.gap: Says the water is gone/dried up into nothing, or only that it sank away, denying the air route.
responseLevels.full: Says the water evaporated into invisible vapour that still exists and can fall again as rain, describing the up-and-back-down loop, and predicts droplets under a covering lid.
responseLevels.partial: Says the water went into the air but treats it as a one-way disappearance — can't say it still exists as vapour or that it returns as rain.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: There was a puddle in the playground yesterday, and today it's gone — but nobody tipped it out or mopped it up. Where did the water go, and is it gone forever?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands evaporation as conservation says the water rose into the air and still exists. A child with the disappearance idea says it 'dried up and is gone'; a child with the soak-only idea insists it all went into the ground — each a distinct, documented tell.
